editorial:
Imagine feeling like you just do not fit in anywhere, especially in a boring town where every house looks the same. That is exactly where you find Evan, a teenager who feels totally worthless at home. He ends up running away and joining a group of other lost kids who have been tossed aside by their families. They form their own little makeshift family in a squat, trying to survive and find some joy through music and friendship. The vibe is raw and gritty, making you feel the desperation of these kids who just want someone to love them and a place to call home.

What really makes this one work is how real the acting feels. You can tell the director wanted it to look like a documentary, which adds a lot of tension. While the pacing is a bit slow in the middle, the emotional payoff is huge. If you like stories about outcasts and rebellious youth, you should definitely give this a try. Since it is an older film, you might want to track down a remastered 4K Blu-ray for your collection to see the details better, or just rent it on Apple TV for a quick movie night.
endingExplained: The story takes a dark turn when the group's peace is shattered by violence. After a tragic event where one of the friends is killed, the makeshift family falls apart. Evan realizes that running away did not actually fix his problems. The movie ends on a sad note, showing that for some kids, there is no easy way out of their situation and the cycle of pain just keeps going.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves raw stories about outcasts and 80s underground culture.
